name: Non-surgical rhinoplasty (liquid nose job)

lead: Non-surgical rhinoplasty, or a liquid nose job, uses injectable filler to reshape the nose without cutting. Practitioners use it to fill depressions, camouflage a dorsal hump, raise the tip angle or add projection, giving a straighter, better-projected profile that is visible immediately.

A filler, most commonly hyaluronic acid gel, is placed in selected points to change contour by adding volume and creating optical straightening. It can only add volume and does not reduce nose size. The literature is mostly retrospective series and reviews, including a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years.

paras: It is a short clinic treatment with little or no recovery, appealing to people who want a change without surgery. Results from hyaluronic acid fillers are temporary, and the enzyme hyaluronidase can dissolve them.

The nose's vessels connect with the ophthalmic artery, so accidental intravascular injection can cause skin ischaemia and, rarely, vision loss. Other reported effects include swelling, bruising, asymmetry and granulomas. Regulatory approval of fillers varies by product and use.

angle.text: Filler is injected to smooth a bridge bump, lift the tip or add projection without surgery, with the change visible immediately. Results are temporary, and it is seen as a reversible, lower-commitment alternative to surgical rhinoplasty.

lead: Non-surgical rhinoplasty, also called liquid rhinoplasty, is a cosmetic procedure that reshapes the nose with injectable filler instead of surgery.[1] Wikipedia describes it as using fillers such as collagen or hyaluronic acid to fill depressed areas, lift the angle of the tip or smooth bumps on the bridge, without changing the size of the nose.[1]

The technique is described in the plastic-surgery literature as increasingly popular, and has been studied mainly in retrospective series and reviews, such as a single-centre retrospective analysis of a standardised five-point technique and a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years.[2][3] The nose's vascular anatomy, including connections to the ophthalmic artery, makes accidental intra-arterial injection a recognised hazard, and papers have reported vision loss and skin ischaemia and treatment with high-dose hyaluronidase.[4][5]
In looksmaxxing culture it is classed with hardmaxxing procedures as a reversible, lower-commitment alternative to surgical rhinoplasty.
infobox: Mostly hyaluronic acid fillers; others have been used[1][10]
Smooth hump, lift tip, add projection or fill depressions[1]
Temporary; hyaluronic acid filler lasts roughly 6 to 12 months in general[8]
Hyaluronic acid can be dissolved with hyaluronidase[4]
Vascular occlusion with skin necrosis or vision loss[4][5]

paras: The procedure is performed in a clinic with a needle or cannula to place small amounts of filler at defined points along the nose, such as the dorsum, radix and tip.[3][6] Published methods include a five-point technique, a deep columellar approach, and a 'five-principle, five-step' method.[3][6][7] Wikipedia notes that the technique is limited to adding volume and cannot reduce nasal size.[1]
Early attempts at nasal soft-tissue augmentation used paraffin wax and silicone, which Wikipedia describes as harmful, and physicians shifted to modern fillers after about 2000.[1]

A retrospective single-centre analysis of a five-point technique assessed safety and effectiveness for insufficient projection and other indications in adult patients.[3] Surgeons describe results as temporary, with hyaluronic acid filler in general lasting about 6 to 12 months.[8] Non-surgical rhinoplasty is considered in reviews of dorsal augmentation as an alternative to graft-based surgery, which carries its own complication risks.[9]

A review of safety in nasal filler use and a study of the ultrasound anatomy of the dorsal nasal artery address how vessel location relates to risk.[2][5] The nose's blood supply communicates with the ophthalmic artery via branches of the facial artery, so accidental injection into a vessel can cause skin ischaemia and, rarely, partial or complete vision loss.[4]

A 2019 case report in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery described reversal of post-filler vision loss and skin ischaemia with high-dose pulsed hyaluronidase injections.[4] Wikipedia's page on hyaluronic acid lists erythema, itching, pain, bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomatous reactions among filler complications.[8]
The procedure is categorised among hardmaxxing options that people consider as a trial run for surgical rhinoplasty or as an alternative to it. Specific forum threads are not cited here.

Published evidence consists mainly of retrospective series, technique descriptions, anatomical studies and complication case reports rather than randomised trials. A retrospective analysis of a five-point technique reported safety and effectiveness outcomes,[3] and a case series of 511 procedures over 16 years described a deep columellar approach.[6] Reviews of nonsurgical rhinoplasty and of liquid rhinoplasty summarise techniques and complications.[10][11] The complication literature includes a case report of vision-loss reversal with hyaluronidase.[4]

timeline.event: After about 2000, physicians shift from paraffin and silicone to modern fillers for nasal augmentation, according to Wikipedia.[1]
